source.title: Find the Maximum Length of a Good Subsequence I

teaching.hint: What determines the extra cost of appending a new chosen element?

solution_outline.decisive_insight: The last chosen value determines whether an append consumes one change, so last index plus remaining change allowance is sufficient state.
solution_outline.approach: For each ending index and budget, keep the greatest subsequence length. Try every earlier ending index: extending an equal value spends zero changes; extending a different value spends one. Start with singleton length one and maximize over endpoints at budget k.
solution_outline.state_and_invariant: The state for index i and allowance c is the longest subsequence ending at i with at most c changes; every predecessor comes from a smaller index.
solution_outline.correctness: Every nonsingleton subsequence has one penultimate index. Removing its last element reduces the allowed change count by exactly the equality-dependent transition cost. All such predecessor cases are considered, and appending to any recorded predecessor realizes a valid candidate. Induction over endpoints therefore yields exact optima; maximizing their k-allowance states covers every valid final endpoint.
solution_outline.complexity: O(n²(k+1)) time and O(n(k+1)) auxiliary space, including the k=0 case.
solution_outline.pitfall: Changes are between successive chosen elements, not distinct values; returning to a prior value can consume another change.

common_wrong_turns: Changes are between successive chosen elements, not distinct values; returning to a prior value can consume another change.
source_fidelity_notes: Omitted both incorrect source example explanations; retained the formal change rule and independently derived [1,2,1], k=1 example.
